history.heading: Crossroads of empires
paragraphs: The lands of present-day Afghanistan sit where Central Asia, South Asia and the Iranian plateau meet, and for thousands of years they lay on major trade routes, including the Silk Road. The region was part of the Persian Achaemenid Empire, was conquered by Alexander the Great in the 4th century BCE, and later became a centre of Greco-Buddhist culture under the Kushan Empire, which left monuments such as the giant Buddhas of Bamiyan.

Islam arrived from the 7th century onward. The region was ruled by a succession of dynasties, including the Ghaznavids and Ghurids, before suffering the Mongol invasions of the 13th century. Herat flourished as a centre of art and learning under the Timurids in the 15th century, and the Mughal Empire was founded by Babur, who began his conquest of India from Kabul.

history.heading: Birth of the Afghan state
paragraphs: Modern Afghanistan is usually dated to 1747, when Ahmad Shah Durrani united Pashtun tribes and founded an empire stretching from Iran to northern India. In the 19th century the country became a buffer in the "Great Game" between the British and Russian empires and fought three wars with Britain.

After the Third Anglo-Afghan War in 1919, Afghanistan gained full control of its foreign affairs. King Amanullah attempted rapid modernisation in the 1920s but faced a conservative backlash. The long reign of Zahir Shah (1933–1973) was a period of relative stability and cautious reform, including a 1964 constitution.

history.heading: Decades of war
paragraphs: The monarchy was overthrown in 1973, and a communist coup followed in 1978. The Soviet Union invaded in 1979 to support the communist government, starting a decade-long war against mujahideen resistance groups backed by the United States, Pakistan and others. Millions of Afghans became refugees.

After Soviet withdrawal in 1989 and the fall of the communist government in 1992, rival mujahideen factions fought a civil war. The Taliban, a militant Islamist movement, captured Kabul in 1996 and imposed a strict interpretation of Islamic law, while sheltering al-Qaeda.

history.heading: From 2001 to the present
paragraphs: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, a US-led coalition toppled the Taliban government. An internationally backed Islamic Republic was established, with elections, a new constitution and expanded rights for women, but it struggled with corruption, insurgency and dependence on foreign aid.

Following a 2020 agreement between the United States and the Taliban, foreign troops withdrew, and the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021. They re-established the Islamic Emirate, and their rule has been marked by severe restrictions on women and girls, including bans on secondary and university education.

culture.heading: Peoples and languages
paragraphs: Afghanistan is ethnically diverse. The largest groups are Pashtuns, Tajiks, Hazaras and Uzbeks, along with Turkmens, Aimaqs, Baloch and others. Dari (Afghan Persian) and Pashto are the official languages, and many Afghans speak several languages.
Islam is central to Afghan life; the large majority of the population is Sunni Muslim, with a significant Shia minority, mainly among the Hazaras.

culture.heading: Literature and arts
paragraphs: Poetry holds a special place in Afghan culture. The Persian-language mystic poet Rumi was born in Balkh, and Pashto poets such as Khushal Khan Khattak and Rahman Baba are widely loved. Recitation of poetry and storytelling remain popular.

Afghanistan has rich traditions in carpet weaving, calligraphy, miniature painting and music, including the rubab, a lute-like instrument often called the national instrument. Many forms of music and public art have been restricted under Taliban rule.

culture.heading: Food and traditions
paragraphs: Afghan cuisine features rice dishes such as kabuli pulao, made with carrots, raisins and lamb, along with dumplings (mantu and ashak), kebabs, flatbread (naan) and green tea. Hospitality towards guests is an important value.

Nowruz, the Persian New Year in March, is traditionally celebrated, alongside the Islamic holidays of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. Buzkashi, a rugged horseback game in which riders compete to carry a goat carcass, is a national sport, and cricket has become very popular.

politics.heading: Taliban rule
paragraphs: Since August 2021, Afghanistan has been governed by the Taliban as the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. Power is concentrated in the movement's supreme leader, based in Kandahar, who rules by decree, with a cabinet in Kabul. There is no constitution in force, no elected parliament and no legal opposition.

The Taliban apply a strict interpretation of Sharia law. Women have been barred from most work, from secondary and higher education, and from many public spaces, policies that have drawn wide international condemnation.

politics.heading: International position
paragraphs: Very few countries have formally recognised the Taliban government; Russia became the first to do so in 2025. Many states, including neighbours such as China, Pakistan and Iran, maintain practical relations with it. Afghanistan's seat at the United Nations has remained with representatives of the former government.

Key issues include security threats from groups such as the Islamic State's regional branch, tensions with Pakistan over cross-border militancy, the return of refugees from Iran and Pakistan, and the conditions attached to humanitarian aid.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Afghanistan is one of the poorest countries in the world. Most people depend on agriculture and livestock, growing wheat, fruits, nuts and saffron. The country also holds large untapped deposits of minerals such as copper, iron, lithium and rare earths.

For decades, illicit opium poppy cultivation was a major source of income; Afghanistan was the world's largest producer until the Taliban banned cultivation in 2022, after which production fell sharply.

economy.heading: Crisis since 2021
paragraphs: The 2021 takeover triggered an economic collapse as foreign aid, which had funded most of the government's budget, was cut off, central bank reserves abroad were frozen, and the banking system was disrupted. Widespread hunger followed, and the country depends heavily on humanitarian assistance.

The currency is the afghani. The authorities have focused on trade with neighbours, mining deals and transit projects, but the economy remains fragile, with high unemployment and restrictions on women's work further limiting growth.
